title: Access Specifiers: public and private
learningObjectives: Explain access specifiers: public and private.
Trace member access and function behavior.
Recognize common design or access mistakes.
Create a small structured type with appropriate operations.

understand.concept: public members are accessible through the interface; private members can only be accessed by class member functions and authorized friends. class defaults to private; struct defaults to public.
understand.whyItMatters: Access control protects invariants and discourages direct state manipulation.
understand.explain: Expose needed operations, keep implementation fields private, and avoid unnecessary friend access.

examples.title: Private field and public getter
examples.code: class Account{public:int balance()const{return amount;}private:int amount=0;};\nAccount a;std::cout<<a.balance();
examples.explanation: Private data is accessed through a public method.

examples.title: Set through method
examples.code: class Box{public:void setSize(int n){if(n>0)size=n;}int getSize()const{return size;}private:int size=1;};
examples.explanation: The setter validates before changing private state.

examples.title: Access defaults
examples.explanation: struct members default public; class members default private.

examples.title: Reject direct private access
examples.code: class User{private:int age=20;};\n// User u; u.age is not accessible
examples.explanation: Private members cannot be accessed directly from outside.

examples.title: Public interface
examples.code: class Toggle{public:void flip(){active=!active;}bool isActive()const{return active;}private:bool active=false;};

practise.guidedTask: Trace each Access Specifiers: public and private example. Identify each object, member, access path and initialization value. Describe how the object state changes.
practise.independentTask: Create a small C++ program that models access specifiers: public and private in a realistic scenario. Include appropriate initialization, operations, input validation where needed, and tests for typical and boundary values.
hints: Define the type before creating its objects.
Use dot for objects and arrow for pointers.
Keep fields private when enforcing invariants.
Test object creation and member operations.

questions.explanation: Public members can be accessed by clients.
Private members are not directly accessible externally.
